title: Attention is love
hookLine: Simone Weil held that attention is the rarest, purest form of generosity

cards: Two people at a café table. One is telling a story that matters to her: a diagnosis in the family, a fear she hasn't said out loud before.
The other is nodding, saying mm-hm, and glancing every few seconds at the phone face-up beside the coffee. Nothing rude has been said. Nobody has left.

And still something is missing from that table, and both of them can feel it. A French philosopher named Simone Weil had a word for what's missing, and she ranked it very high among the things one person can give another.

teach.b: In a letter to a friend, Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. Not money, not advice, not even kind words. Attention.

One way to read her: rare because it's hard to give, pure because it asks nothing back. In an essay on school studies, she describes students who think they're paying attention because they frown and tense their muscles.
Real attention is closer to waiting: the mind emptied, open, ready to receive what's actually there, instead of rushing in with its own ideas.

In that same essay, she says that love of neighbor, in its fullness, means being able to ask someone what they are going through, and to really look at the person suffering, not as a case or an example, but as a human being exactly like ourselves.
Weil, who was deeply drawn to Christianity, believed this kind of attention was close to prayer. But you don't need her faith to try it.
Back at the café table, it might look like turning the phone face-down, and letting the other person's story be the only thing in the room.

how: Readers of Simone Weil practice attention as a kind of open, patient waiting: setting aside distractions to listen fully to another person, which she linked to love of neighbor and to prayer.

o: a researcher who studied lifelong friendships
a French philosopher who called attention generosity
a French nun who found a little way of love

games.q: what's inside Weil's idea — tap the pairs.
p: asking what are you going through?

s: for Weil, paying attention means frowning and tensing up
she says that isn't it; real attention is closer to open waiting.
Weil linked attention to love of neighbor
love of neighbor means being able to ask: what are you going through?
Weil said attention is a lesser gift than money
she called attention the rarest and purest form of generosity.

games.q: a friend is telling you something that matters. your phone buzzes. what does Weil's idea point to?
o: check it quickly; you can still nod.
turn it face-down and let their story fill the room.
offer advice so the talk ends sooner.
games.why: for Weil, attention is the rarest, purest generosity: open, waiting, asking what they're going through.

practice: Practice the waiting kind of attention on one simple thing in front of you, your breath, a sound in the room, the light on a wall, without gripping it or frowning at it, letting it come to you the way you'd wait for someone to finish a sentence.
When your mind runs ahead, notice, and come back to waiting; then, before the bell, bring to mind one person who could use five minutes of this attention from you.

wordCard.voice: Simone Weil. The French philosopher who called attention the rarest and purest form of generosity, close to love itself. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: what they are going through. That ends a week of love's names: gladness, an even heart, ren, care for other people's families, a home port, relationships, and now attention. Seven days, seven names.

sources.ref: Simone Weil, letter to Joë Bousquet
Simone Weil, 'Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies with a View to the Love of God'
